provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Augustine's Confessions, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Pusey 1838; Watts 1631) and checked against the Latin; modern critical translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, book by book.
sourcesCited: Latin, the original text of the Confessiones
E. B. Pusey, The Confessions of S. Augustine (1838, public domain)
F. J. Sheed (1942, consulted, not quoted)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Augustine's Confessions in plain modern English that keeps its prayerful urgency and restless intelligence — sin and conversion, memory and time, a heart that finds no rest until it rests in God — while shedding the archaic diction.
introduction: The Confessions is the first true autobiography of an inner life: Augustine talking directly to God, and letting us overhear. It moves from a misspent youth through a long intellectual and moral struggle to conversion, then turns to memory, time, and the meaning of Genesis. Read it as one long prayer thinking out loud.

divergences.phrase: fecisti nos ad te, et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te
divergences.older: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee
divergences.lectio: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you
divergences.note: The most famous sentence in the book and arguably in Western devotional prose. We keep it almost verbatim, shedding only the archaic "madest / repose / Thee." "Restless" is the right modern word for inquietum (restless, unquiet, unsettled), and "rests in you" preserves the requies / requiescat root that anchors the whole work's arc. Nothing here is modernized away; this line is load-bearing and stays plain and strange.

divergences.phrase: fornicabar abs te / amicitia enim huius mundi fornicatio est abs te
divergences.older: I committed fornication against Thee ... the friendship of this world is fornication against Thee
divergences.lectio: I committed adultery against you ... friendship with this world is adultery against you
divergences.note: Augustine's verb is the deliberately scandalous fornicari, echoing the prophets' charge that Israel "plays the harlot" by loving the world instead of God (cf. James 4:4, "friendship of the world is enmity with God"). "Fornication" now reads either clinical or quaint; "adultery" keeps the covenant-betrayal force — the soul is breaking faith with a God it is bound to — which is the metaphor's whole point. We chose betrayal-of-marriage over a generic "unfaithfulness" to preserve the sexual sting Augustine intends.

divergences.phrase: et flebam Didonem extinctam ... at non flebam, quod ipse moriebar
divergences.older: to weep for dead Dido, because she killed herself for love ... weeping not his own death for want of love to Thee
divergences.lectio: to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love ... but does not weep for his own death, dying for want of love for you
divergences.note: The Dido set-piece is the emotional engine of the book's second half: Augustine indicts his boyhood self for shedding real tears over a fictional queen's suicide while feeling nothing for his own soul's death. We keep "Dido," the Virgilian frame, and the brutal symmetry (weeping for her death / not weeping for his) intact rather than smoothing it into abstraction, because the rhetorical mirror IS the argument.

divergences.phrase: foeda erat, et amavi eam; amavi perire, amavi defectum meum
divergences.older: It was foul, and I loved it; I loved to perish, I loved mine own fault (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: It was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own undoing; I loved my falling-away — not the thing I fell toward, but the fall itself.
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole book: sin loved for its own sake. The Latin defectus is privative — a falling-short, a defecting-away from being toward nothing. Pusey's 'fault' loses the metaphysics; 'falling-away / undoing' keeps the sense that the soul loved its own diminishment, not any object. Deliberately left strange.

divergences.phrase: gratis malus … nulla causa malitiae meae nisi malitia mea
divergences.older: that I should be gratuitously evil, having no temptation to ill, but the ill itself
divergences.lectio: that I should be evil for nothing, with no cause for my malice but malice itself
divergences.note: 'Gratuitously evil' is the famous tag, but in modern English 'gratuitous' has drifted toward 'excessive/uncalled-for.' 'Evil for nothing' restores gratis — done for free, with no payoff — which is exactly Augustine's puzzle: motiveless malice. The doubling malitia/malitia is kept as 'malice … malice itself.'

divergences.phrase: foeda eram, et eram in oculis tuis
divergences.older: my beauty consumed away, and I stank in Thine eyes (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: My beauty wasted away, and I was rotten in your eyes
divergences.note: Pusey's vivid 'I stank' overtranslates; the Latin says simply 'I was foul' (foeda), the same root as the theft passage, binding the book together. 'Rotten' keeps the strong sensory disgust and the verbal echo of foeda without inventing a smell the Latin does not name. Direct address kept: 'Thine' → 'your.'

divergences.phrase: a cauldron of shameful loves seethed and crackled in my ears
divergences.older: there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: a cauldron of shameful loves seethed and crackled in my ears
divergences.note: Augustine's Latin puns: sartago (a frying-pan or cauldron) chimes with Carthago, and circumstrepebat means it crackled and roared all around — the very sound of frying. The pun cannot survive translation, but we keep the seething, sizzling cookpot rather than Pusey's gentler 'sang,' since the noise of the cauldron is load-bearing. The famous opening 'To Carthage I came' is preserved.

divergences.phrase: the love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means
divergences.older: the love of wisdom is in Greek called 'philosophy' (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means
divergences.note: The Hortensius turning point. We keep the etymology explicit (philo- + sophia = love of wisdom) because Augustine's whole conversion here pivots on it: a pagan book about loving wisdom turns his prayers toward God. The book's title (Hortensius) and Cicero are preserved untouched.

divergences.phrase: It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish
divergences.older: it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish
divergences.note: The bishop's reply to Monica, Latin 'fieri non potest, ut filius istarum lacrimarum pereat' — one of the most quoted lines in the book. Kept almost verbatim; only the archaic phrasing is smoothed. 'The son of these tears' is preserved exactly, since the whole force depends on it.

divergences.phrase: factus eram ipse mihi magna quaestio
divergences.older: I became a great riddle to myself (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had become a great riddle to myself
divergences.note: One of the most quoted sentences in the book, and the seed of Augustine's whole inward turn: in grief the self becomes opaque to itself. Latin quaestio is literally a "question" or "problem," but Pusey's "riddle" is exactly right — it keeps the sense that Augustine has become a thing he cannot read or answer. We keep it almost verbatim, shifting only the tense to the English pluperfect so it sits naturally in the surrounding narration. Deliberately left strange and unsoftened; nothing is added or explained away.

divergences.phrase: portabam enim concisam et cruentam animam meam, impatientem portari a me
divergences.older: For I bore about a shattered and bleeding soul, impatient of being borne by me (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: For I was carrying my soul, broken and bleeding, and it could not bear to be carried by me
divergences.note: The most physically violent image of grief in the book: the self is split in two, one part lugging the other like a wound. We keep the carrying and the blood intact (concisa = cut to pieces, cruenta = bloodied) rather than abstracting it into "distress." Pusey's "impatient of being borne" is accurate but archaic; "could not bear to be carried" preserves the bitter pun on bearing/carrying a burden that the soul itself refuses. The strangeness is load-bearing and stays.

divergences.phrase: fuderam in harenam animam meam diligendo moriturum acsi non moriturum
divergences.older: I had poured out my soul upon the dust, in loving one that must die, as if he would never die (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had poured out my soul upon the sand, in loving one who must die as though he would never die
divergences.note: The diagnostic line of the whole book of grief: the error was not love but the lie inside it — loving a mortal thing as though it were immortal. Augustine returns to this thought as the cure (love souls in God, who cannot be lost). Pusey's "dust" renders harena, but harena is specifically sand — the ground that swallows water and gives nothing back, the right image for a love poured out and lost. We keep the bare, aphoristic shape ("one who must die as though he would never die") because the symmetry is the argument; it is not smoothed into a general remark about loss.

divergences.phrase: Faustus quidam ... magnus laqueus diaboli
divergences.older: a certain Bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the Devil (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: a certain bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the devil
divergences.note: Kept almost verbatim, because it is load-bearing and meant to unsettle: the most celebrated teacher in Augustine's old sect is introduced not as a fraud but as a genuinely charming, decent man — and named outright as the devil's trap. The strangeness is the point, so we hold to "a great snare of the devil" and let the seductive smooth-tongued bishop (and, later, the man Augustine comes to like for his honest admission of ignorance) stand under that verdict. Only the archaic capitalization and inversion are smoothed; the image is not softened into "temptation" or "danger."

divergences.phrase: et mentitus sum matri, et illi matri, et evasi
divergences.older: And I lied to my mother, and such a mother, and escaped (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: So I lied to my mother, and to a mother like that, and got away.
divergences.note: The hinge of the book and one of its most painful confessions: Augustine slips away by night from the harbor at Carthage, leaving Monica praying at Cyprian's shrine, having told her he was only seeing a friend off. The Latin doubles matri — "to my mother, and to THAT mother" — the repetition driving home that it was not just any deception but the betrayal of the one person praying for his soul. We keep the doubling intact ("to my mother, and to a mother like that") rather than collapsing it, because the verbal stab is the confession. "Got away" preserves the furtive evasi over a flatter "escaped."

divergences.phrase: suscepit me paterne ille homo Dei ... ut ab illo ad te scienter ducerer
divergences.older: That man of God received me as a father ... that by him I might knowingly be led to Thee (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: That man of God received me like a father ... that by him I might knowingly be led to you.
divergences.note: The turn of the whole book. Augustine comes to Milan still a Manichee, despairing of the Catholic Church, drawn only by curiosity about Ambrose's reputation as an orator — and Ambrose simply receives him with fatherly kindness. We keep "like a father" and the deliberate play of unknowing/knowing (led "all unknowing" to Ambrose, that through Ambrose he might "knowingly" be led to God), because the quiet, undramatic welcome is exactly the hinge on which the conversion narrative will swing in Books VI–VIII. Nothing is heightened; the plainness of the reception is its force.

divergences.phrase: laetitia temporalis felicitatis
divergences.older: the joy of a temporary felicity ... he verily had not the true joy; but yet I with those my ambitious designs was seeking one much less true
divergences.lectio: the joy of a little patch of happiness ... His joy was not the true joy, of course; but the joy I was after, with all my ambitious designs, was a far less true one still
divergences.note: This is the moral hinge of Book VI: the drunken beggar, merry on a few begged coins, is happier than the ambitious Augustine sweating toward an emperor's panegyric he knows is a lie. The strangeness is load-bearing and must not be softened — the beggar genuinely is "beyond" Augustine, "the happier" man. We keep the brutal comparison intact (he cheerful / I anxious; he free of care / I full of fears) and preserve Augustine's own verdict that his glory was the less true of the two false joys. Pusey's "felicity" is dead vocabulary; "a little patch of happiness" keeps the smallness and contingency of temporal felicitas without inventing anything.

divergences.locus: VI.xii (Pusey seg. 27), Alypius at the amphitheater
divergences.phrase: ut vidit illum sanguinem, immanitatem simul ebibit ... hauriebat furias
divergences.older: For so soon as he saw that blood, he therewith drunk down savageness; nor turned away, but fixed his eye, drinking in frenzy, unawares, and was delighted with that guilty fight, and intoxicated with the bloody pastime
divergences.lectio: The moment he saw the blood, he drank down savagery with it, and did not turn away, but fixed his gaze, and drank in the frenzy without knowing it, taking delight in that guilty contest, drunk on the bloody pleasure
divergences.note: The most famous image in the book outside the pear theft: Alypius, dragged to the games with his eyes shut, opens them at the crowd's roar and is wounded deeper in soul than the gladiator in body. Augustine's metaphor is relentlessly liquid — ebibit (drank down), hauriebat (kept drawing/draining in), inebriabatur (was made drunk). We keep every beat of the drinking-in-of-blood image rather than abstracting it to "was corrupted," because the physiology of the addiction — savagery swallowed like wine — is the whole point. "Drinking in the savagery" is the load-bearing strangeness the brief names explicitly.

divergences.locus: VI.xv (Pusey seg. 24), the dismissal of the concubine
divergences.phrase: avulsa a latere meo ... concubina, cor, ubi adhaerebat, concisum et vulneratum mihi erat et trahebat sanguinem
divergences.older: my concubine being torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding
divergences.lectio: the woman I lived with was torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, and my heart, which clung to her, was torn and wounded and left bleeding
divergences.note: Augustine never names her, and we keep her unnamed, as the original withholds the name — the omission is itself a wound the text carries. "Concubine" in modern English reads either legalistic or lurid and obscures that this was a years-long partnership and the mother of his son; "the woman I lived with" restores the human fact without softening the moral verdict Augustine passes on himself (he was "a slave to lust," not a "lover of marriage"). The torn / wounded / bleeding triad (concisum, vulneratum, trahebat sanguinem) is kept verbatim in force: the rawest emotional sentence in the book, and it must keep its blood.

divergences.locus: Book VII.x (Pusey seg. 15), the vision of the Light
divergences.phrase: et inveni longe me esse a te in regione dissimilitudinis ... ego sum qui sum
divergences.older: I perceived myself to be far off from Thee, in the region of unlikeness, as if I heard this Thy voice from on high ... Yet verily, I AM that I AM (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I found that I was far away from you, in the region of unlikeness ... No — truly, I AM WHO I AM
divergences.note: The summit of the book's intellectual ascent, where the Neoplatonic climb meets the God of Exodus. Two phrases are load-bearing and must not be smoothed. "Region of unlikeness" (regio dissimilitudinis) is a technical Platonic term — the soul's distance from God measured as ontological un-likeness, not mere geography — and we keep it exactly, strange as it sounds, because it names Augustine's whole diagnosis of the fallen self. And "I AM WHO I AM" (the burning-bush name, Exod. 3:14) is kept verbatim in small capitals: the answer is not an argument but a Name, and the force depends on its bareness. We render Pusey's "I AM that I AM" with the more standard "I AM WHO I AM" but add nothing and explain nothing away.

divergences.locus: Book VII.xii (Pusey seg. 17), evil as privation
divergences.phrase: quaesivi quid esset iniquitas, et non inveni substantiam, sed ... omne quod corrumpitur privatur bono
divergences.older: all which is corrupted is deprived of good ... That evil then which I sought, whence it is, is not any substance (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: everything that is corrupted is being robbed of some good ... that evil whose origin I was searching for is not a substance
divergences.note: The metaphysical heart of Book VII and Augustine's lifelong answer to the Manichees: evil is not a thing (substantia) but a privation, a robbing-away of good. The argument is precise and must not be flattened into a vague "evil is the absence of good." We keep the active, almost violent privatur as "is being robbed of some good" rather than a static "is deprived," because Augustine's point is dynamic — corruption is a process that diminishes a real good, and a thing wholly stripped of good would simply cease to be. The conclusion ("evil is not a substance") is kept bare and load-bearing; the whole theodicy turns on it.

divergences.phrase: quaerebam viam comparandi roboris ... non tenebam ... donec amplecterer mediatorem ... Verbum caro factum est
divergences.older: Then I sought a way of obtaining strength sufficient to enjoy Thee; and found it not, until I embraced that Mediator betwixt God and men ... For, the Word was made flesh (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I began to search for a way to gain the strength I needed to enjoy you, and I did not find it — not until I embraced that Mediator between God and men ... For the Word was made flesh
divergences.note: This is the hinge on which all of Book VII turns: the Platonists could lift Augustine to glimpse Being, but could not give him the strength to stay — only the Incarnation could, the Word stooping into flesh as "milk for our infancy." We keep "Mediator" (mediator, 1 Tim. 2:5) as a title, not softened to "go-between," and we keep "the Word was made flesh" verbatim (John 1:14), the load-bearing answer to everything the Platonist books lacked. The whole book is built so that this plain sentence lands with full weight after pages of metaphysics; nothing here is modernized away.

divergences.phrase: da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo
divergences.older: Give me chastity and continency, only not yet (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Give me chastity and self-control — only not yet
divergences.note: The most quoted prayer in the book, and one of the most honest sentences ever written about a divided will: Augustine begs God for chastity while secretly dreading to be heard, because he wants the disease of lust "fed full rather than snuffed out" (malebam expleri quam exstingui). We keep the prayer almost verbatim, since its whole force is in the bald confession of the trick the heart plays on itself. We render continentia as "self-control" rather than the now-archaic "continency," but the load-bearing punchline — "only not yet" — is kept exactly. Nothing is softened; the strangeness is the confession.

divergences.phrase: tolle, lege; tolle, lege
divergences.older: Take up and read; Take up and read (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Take up and read, take up and read
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole Confessions: the child's chant in the neighboring house that sends Augustine to the book of Paul. The Latin "Tolle, lege" is so famous it is often left untranslated, and we preserve it as a touchstone here while rendering the chant itself in plain English. "Take up and read" is the load-bearing line and is kept exactly as Pusey has it (and as the tradition has fixed it), because the entire conversion turns on those four words and the verse they send him to — Romans 13:13–14, which we also keep close to the literal ("put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh and its cravings"). Nothing here is modernized away.

divergences.phrase: imperat animus corpori, et paretur statim; imperat animus sibi, et resistitur
divergences.older: The mind commands the body, and it obeys instantly; the mind commands itself, and is resisted (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: The mind commands the body, and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself, and is resisted
divergences.note: The most influential piece of psychology in the book, and the heart of Augustine's analysis of the will that cannot obey itself: a single will, not two natures, half willing and half not, and so tearing itself apart. We keep the bare, antithetical shape (commands the body / is obeyed; commands itself / is resisted) verbatim in force, because the symmetry is the argument — it is this passage, not Manichaean dualism, that explains the agony in the garden. Pusey's "and it obeys instantly" we render as "and is obeyed at once" to match the passive of the matching clause ("and is resisted") and let the parallel ring. Deliberately left plain and strange; nothing is added or explained away.

divergences.locus: IX.10 (Pusey segs. 22–25), the vision at Ostia
divergences.phrase: et dum loquimur et inhiamus illi, attingimus eam modice toto ictu cordis
divergences.older: And while we were discoursing and panting after her, we slightly touched on her with the whole effort of our heart (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: And while we were speaking and panting after her, we touched her, a little, with one whole stroke of the heart
divergences.note: The climax of the book and one of the summits of Western mystical prose: mother and son, leaning at a window in Ostia, rise "step by step" through created things to the eternal Wisdom and brush against her for a single instant. The crux is ictu cordis. Pusey's "the whole effort of our heart" loses the decisive image: ictus is a single beat, blow, or stroke — the touch lasts exactly one heartbeat. We keep "one whole stroke of the heart" so the reader feels both the totality of the reach (toto, the whole self thrown into it) and its momentariness (one beat, then gone). We deliberately keep the strange Wisdom-as-"she" and the bare grammar of eternity ("only 'is'") rather than smoothing them; the passage's holiness is in its difficulty, and nothing in it is paraphrased away.

divergences.phrase: ponite hoc corpus ubicumque; nihil vos eius cura conturbet; tantum illud vos rogo, ut ad domini altare memineritis mei, ubiubi fueritis
divergences.older: Lay this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Lay this body anywhere; let no care for it trouble you in the least. This one thing only I ask: that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you may be.
divergences.note: Monica, who had spent her life preparing a grave beside her husband in Africa, lets the whole earthly wish drop in a single sentence — the inward fruit of the vision she has just shared. The line is load-bearing and must stay almost verbatim; we shed only the archaic grammar ("disquiet you," "wherever you be") and keep the flat, astonishing "anywhere" (ubicumque) and the one thing she does still want — to be named at the altar. The repetition ubiubi ("wherever, wherever") is rendered plainly as "wherever you may be," matching the deliberate plainness of her dying speech. Nothing is added or softened; the renunciation is exactly as stark as Augustine wrote it.

divergences.phrase: ne reprehendat me, si aliquantulum temporis matrem... flevi, matrem... quae me multos annos fleverat, ut oculis tuis viverem
divergences.older: if he finds sin therein, that I wept my mother for a small portion of an hour (the mother who... had for many years wept for me that I might live in Thine eyes), let him not deride me (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for one small fraction of an hour — the mother who for the time was dead to my eyes, who for so many years had wept for me that I might live in your eyes — let him not mock me
divergences.note: Augustine has spent the whole death-scene damming his tears — at the deathbed, at the prayers, at the graveside — until, alone in bed, he finally lets them "flow as freely as they would." The crux is the symmetry of weeping that closes it: he weeps for his mother for a fraction of an hour; she had wept for him for years, that he might live. This is the same logic as Book III's "the son of these tears," and the mirror is the argument, so we keep it exact: his brief tears against her long ones, his eyes against your eyes (oculis tuis). Pusey's "a small portion of an hour" is kept in sense as "one small fraction of an hour"; we do not round it off or generalize the grief, because its smallness, set against her years, is the point Augustine is confessing.

segments.text: You are great, Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is your power, and your wisdom has no measure. And a human being wants to praise you — one small piece of your creation, a man who carries his own death about with him, who carries the evidence of his sin and the evidence that you stand against the proud. Still he wants to praise you, this small piece of your creation. You yourself stir him to take delight in praising you, because you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand which comes first: to call on you or to praise you? And again — to know you or to call on you? For how can anyone call on you without knowing you? Not knowing you, he might call on something other than you. Or is it rather that we call on you in order to know you? But how can they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe without someone to preach? Those who seek the Lord will praise him, for those who seek will find him, and those who find will praise him. Let me seek you, Lord, by calling on you, and call on you by believing in you — for you have been preached to us. My faith calls on you, Lord, the faith you gave me, the faith you breathed into me through the coming of your Son in the flesh, through the work of the one who preached him.

And how shall I call upon my God — my God and my Lord — since to call him is to call him into myself? What room is there inside me for my God to come, the God who made heaven and earth? Is there really anything in me, Lord my God, that can hold you? Can heaven and earth, which you made, and in which you made me, hold you? Or is it that, because nothing could exist without you, whatever exists holds you? Then since I too exist, why do I beg you to come into me, when I would not exist at all unless you were already in me? For I am not yet in hell — and yet you are there too. If I go down into hell, you are there. I could not exist, my God, could not exist at all, unless you were in me; or rather, unless I were in you, from whom all things come, through whom all things come, in whom all things hold together. Yes, Lord, exactly so. Where do I call you to, since I am already in you? And from where could you enter me — for where can I go beyond heaven and earth, so that from there my God might come into me, the God who said, I fill heaven and earth?

Do heaven and earth contain you, then, since you fill them? Or do you fill them and still overflow, since they cannot contain you? And when heaven and earth are full, where do you pour the rest of yourself? Or do you have no need of anything to contain you, since you contain all things — filling what you fill by holding it? The vessels you fill do not hold you up: even if they shatter, you are not spilled. And when you pour yourself out on us, you do not fall down — you lift us up. You are not scattered — you gather us together. But when you fill all things, do you fill them with the whole of yourself? Or, since all things cannot hold the whole of you, do they hold only a part — and all of them the same part at once? Or each its own part, the larger things more, the smaller less? Then is one part of you greater and another smaller? Or are you wholly everywhere, while nothing holds the whole of you?

What are you, then, my God? What, but the Lord God? For who is Lord but the Lord, who is God but our God? Highest and best, most powerful, all-powerful; most merciful and most just; most hidden and most present; most beautiful and most strong; steady, and beyond our grasp; unchanging, yet changing all things; never new, never old, yet making all things new — and bringing old age on the proud, who never notice it. Always working, always at rest; gathering, yet lacking nothing; carrying, filling, sheltering; creating, feeding, bringing to ripeness; always seeking, though you have everything. You love, but without the fever of it; you are jealous, but without anxiety; you regret, but feel no grief; you are angry, yet stay serene; you change your works while your purpose never changes; you take back what you find, though you never lost it; you are never in need, yet you are glad of gains; never greedy, yet you charge interest. We pay you more than we owe, so that you become our debtor — yet who has anything that is not already yours? You pay debts though you owe nothing; you forgive debts and lose nothing. And what have I now said, my God, my life, my holy joy? What does anyone say when he speaks of you? Yet woe to those who say nothing, since even the most eloquent are struck dumb.

Oh, let me rest in you! Let you come into my heart and make it drunk, so that I forget my troubles and embrace you, my one good. What are you to me? In your pity, teach me to say it. What am I to you, that you command me to love you, and are angry with me if I do not, and threaten me with terrible griefs? Is it a small grief, then, not to love you? Oh, for the sake of your mercies, tell me, Lord my God, what you are to me. Say to my soul, I am your salvation. Say it so that I hear it. Look, Lord — my heart is here before you; open its ears and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Let me run after that voice and lay hold of you. Do not hide your face from me. Let me die — so that I do not die — only let me see your face.

The house of my soul is too narrow for you to enter; widen it. It is falling down; rebuild it. It holds things that must offend your eyes; I confess it, I know it. But who will clean it out? To whom but you should I cry? Lord, cleanse me from the faults I cannot see, and keep your servant from the power of the enemy. I believe, and so I speak. Lord, you know. Have I not confessed my wrongs against myself to you, and have you not, my God, forgiven the guilt of my heart? I do not go to law against you, who are the truth; I am afraid of deceiving myself, of letting my own sin lie to itself. So I will not go to law against you — for if you, Lord, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?

Yet let me speak before your mercy — me, dust and ashes. Let me speak, since I am speaking to your mercy and not to a man who would sneer. Perhaps you too look down on me — yet you will turn back and have compassion on me. For what would I say, Lord my God, except that I do not know where I came from when I came into this — what shall I call it — dying life, or living death? The comforts of your compassion took me up at once: I have it from the parents of my flesh, out of whose substance you shaped me in time, for I do not remember it myself. So the comforts of a woman's milk welcomed me. My mother and my nurses did not fill their own breasts; you gave the food of my infancy through them, by the order you have set, by which you hand out your riches through the hidden depths of all things. You also gave me to want no more than you gave, and gave my nurses the will to give me what you had given them. For with an instinct planted by you they wanted to give me what they had in abundance from you. The good I had from them was good for them, too. Yet it was not really from them but through them; for from you, God, come all good things, and from my God comes all my well-being. This I learned later, when you cried out to me through these gifts, inside me and around me. Back then I knew only how to suck, to settle into what pleased me and to cry at whatever hurt my body — nothing more.

Later I began to smile, first in my sleep, then awake. So I was told of myself, and I believed it, for we see the same in other infants, though I do not remember it of myself. Little by little I began to notice where I was, and to want to make my wishes known to those who could meet them — and I could not, for the wishes were inside me, and they were outside, and no sense of theirs could reach into my spirit. So I would fling my limbs and my voice about at random, making the few signs I could, as best I could, that were like — though really very little like — what I wanted. And when I was not obeyed at once (my wishes being either harmful or unintelligible), I was furious at my elders for not giving in to me, at people who owed me nothing for not serving me, and I took revenge on them by crying. That infants are like this, I have learned from watching them; and that I was once like this, they have shown me — these infants who knew nothing of it — better than my nurses, who did.

And look — my infancy died long ago, and I am alive. But you, Lord, live forever, and nothing in you dies; for before the foundation of the worlds, and before everything that can be called "before," you are, and you are God and Lord of all that you have made. In you stand fixed forever the first causes of all unstanding things; in you the springs of all changing things hold unchanging; in you live the eternal reasons of all the reasonless, passing things. Tell me, Lord — I am your suppliant — tell me, you who pity all, for I am pitiable: did my infancy follow some earlier age of mine that died before it? Was that age the time I spent in my mother's womb? Of that I have heard something, and I have myself seen pregnant women. And before that, my God, my joy — what then? Was I anywhere, was I anyone? I have no one to tell me this — not father, not mother, not the experience of others, not my own memory. Do you laugh at me for asking, and tell me instead to praise you and acknowledge you for what I do know?

I acknowledge you, Lord of heaven and earth, and I praise you for the first beginnings of my being and for my infancy, of which I remember nothing — since you have arranged that a person should learn much about himself from others, and believe much on the word of mere women. Even then I existed and was alive, and toward the end of infancy I was already looking for signs by which to make my feelings known to others. Where could such a creature come from, Lord, but from you? Can anyone be his own maker? Is there any other stream from which being and life could flow into us, except from you, Lord, in whom being and life are one? For you yourself are supremely Being and Life. You are most high, and you do not change, and in you today never comes to an end — and yet in you it does come to an end, since all such things are also in you; they would have no way to pass at all unless you held them. And since your years do not fail, your years are one single today. How many of our years, and our fathers' years, have flowed away through your today, taking from it the measure and the shape of whatever being they had — and still others will flow away, and take the shape of their own degree of being. But you stay the same; and all of tomorrow, and all beyond it, and all of yesterday, and all behind that, you have done today. What does it matter to me if someone does not grasp this? Let him rejoice even so, and say, What is this? Let him rejoice, and be content to find you by not finding you out, rather than by finding you out to miss you altogether.

Hear me, God. Alas for the sin of man! So a man says, and you pity him, for you made him, but the sin in him you did not make. Who reminds me of the sins of my infancy? For in your sight no one is free of sin, not even the infant whose life on earth is a single day. Who reminds me? Does not every little child, in whom I see what I no longer remember of myself? What, then, was my sin? Was it that I cried for the breast? If I cried now for food fit to my age, I would rightly be laughed at and corrected. What I did then deserved correction, but since I could not have understood it, neither custom nor reason allowed me to be corrected; for such habits we root out and throw away as we grow. No one who is pruning knowingly throws away what is good. Was it then good, even for a moment, to scream for what would have done me harm if I had got it? To rage bitterly at free people — my own elders, the very authors of my birth — for not serving me? To strike out and try to hurt the many wiser than me who would not obey my every whim, because they would not obey commands that would have harmed me? So the innocence of infants lies in the weakness of their limbs, not in their will. I have seen and known a jealous baby myself: it could not yet speak, but it went pale and looked daggers at the other child at the breast. Everyone knows this. Mothers and nurses say they can soothe it somehow. But is even this innocent — that when the fountain of milk is flowing in plenty, the child will not let another share it, though that other is in the greatest need and its very life depends on it for now? We are gentle with all this, not because it is no evil or only a small one, but because it will pass with the years — for though we tolerate it now, the very same temper is completely unbearable when we find it in grown men.

You, then, Lord my God, who gave life to me in my infancy and fitted the body you gave with senses, set its limbs in order, gave its parts their beauty, and for its general good and safety planted in it all the powers of a living thing — you command me to praise you in these things, to confess to you and sing to your name, Most High. For you are God, almighty and good, even if you had done nothing but this, which no one but you could do — you whose oneness is the pattern of all things, who out of your own beauty make all things beautiful, and order all things by your law. So this age, Lord, of which I have no memory, which I take on others' word and guess at from other infants — true as the guess may be — I am still reluctant to count it as part of this life of mine that I live in this world. For it is as hidden from me, in the shadows of forgetting, as the time I spent in my mother's womb. And if I was shaped in wrongdoing, and in sin my mother conceived me — then where, I beg you, my God, where, Lord, or when, was I, your servant, free of guilt? But there — I let that time go by; what have I now to do with it, when I can recall no trace of it?

Leaving infancy behind, I came to boyhood — or rather it came to me and took the place of infancy. And infancy did not depart (where would it go?), and yet it was no longer there. For I was no longer a speechless infant but a speaking boy. This I remember, and I have since noticed how I learned to speak. It was not that my elders taught me words by any set method, as they soon taught me other lessons. No — longing to make my thoughts known by cries and broken sounds and the various motions of my limbs, so as to get my way, and unable to express all I wanted or to whom I wanted, I drilled the sounds in my memory by the understanding you gave me, my God. When people named some thing and turned toward it as they spoke, I saw it and grasped that the thing they wanted to point out was called by the sound they made. Their meaning was plain from the motion of their bodies — the natural language, you might say, of every nation, made of the face, the glance of the eye, the gestures of the limbs, the tone of the voice, all showing the mind's state as it reaches for things, holds them, refuses them, or shuns them. And so, by hearing words again and again in their places in different sentences, I gradually worked out what they stood for, and having trained my mouth to these signs, I used them to speak my will. So I traded these current coins of our wishes with the people around me, and launched out deeper into the stormy commerce of human life — still under the authority of my parents and the orders of my elders.

O God, my God, what miseries and mockeries I now went through, when as a boy it was set before me that the right thing was to obey my teachers, so that I might get on in this world and excel in the arts of the tongue — which would serve to win the praise of men and false riches. Next I was sent to school to get learning, though I, poor wretch, could not see what it was good for; and yet if I was lazy at it, I was beaten. Our elders judged this right; many before us had marked out the same weary paths, and we were made to tread them, with toil and grief piled on the children of Adam. But, Lord, we found that men called on you, and from them we learned to think of you, as well as we could, as some great One who could hear us and help us, though hidden from our senses. So as a boy I began to pray to you, my help and my refuge, and broke the bonds of my tongue to call on you, and prayed — small as I was, but with no small earnestness — that I might not be beaten at school. And when you did not hear me (which was not to leave me to my folly), my elders, even my own parents, who wished me no harm, laughed at my beatings — which were then my great and grievous trouble.

Is there anyone, Lord, with a soul so great, who clings to you with such fierce love — for a kind of dullness can manage it too — but is there anyone who, from devotion to you, is given so great a spirit that he can make as light of the racks and hooks and other torments that men dread and pray to escape from all over the world, mocking those who fear them most bitterly, as our parents mocked the torments we suffered as boys at our masters' hands? For we feared our torments no less, and prayed no less to you to escape them. And yet we sinned, by writing or reading or studying less than was demanded of us. It was not, Lord, that we lacked memory or ability — your will gave us enough for our age. The trouble was that we loved nothing but play, and for this we were punished by men who were doing the very same. But the idling of grown men is called "business"; when boys do the same, those very men punish them — and no one pities either the boys or the men. For will any sound judge approve of my being beaten as a boy because playing ball kept me from studies I was supposed to learn, so that as a man I might play at worse things? And the one who beat me — what else was he doing? If he came off worse in some petty argument with a fellow teacher, he was more soured and jealous than I was when a playmate beat me at ball.

And yet I did sin in this, Lord God, the maker and the ruler of all things in nature, though of sins only the ruler — I sinned, Lord my God, by disobeying the commands of my parents and my masters. For whatever they wanted me to learn, with whatever motive, I could have put to good use later. I disobeyed not from a better choice but from love of play: I loved the pride of winning my matches, and to have my ears tickled with made-up stories until they itched the more; and the same hunger flashed brighter and brighter in my eyes for the shows and games of grown men. Yet the very people who put on these shows are held in such honor that almost everyone wants the same for their children — and are still glad to have them beaten if those games keep them from the studies by which they hope their children will become the givers of such shows. Look with pity, Lord, on all this, and rescue us who call on you now; rescue too those who do not yet call on you, so that they may call on you, and you may rescue them.

As a boy I had already heard of an eternal life promised us through the humility of the Lord our God, who stooped to our pride; and from my mother's womb — for she greatly hoped in you — I was marked with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt. You saw, Lord, how once, while still a boy, I was suddenly seized with a stomach fever and came close to death — you saw, my God, for you were already my keeper, with what eagerness and faith I begged, from the devout care of my mother and of your Church, the mother of us all, for the baptism of your Christ, my God and Lord. And the mother of my flesh, deeply troubled — for with a heart pure in your faith she was laboring all the harder to give birth to my salvation — would have hurried to have me consecrated and cleansed by the saving sacraments, confessing you, Lord Jesus, for the forgiveness of sins, had I not suddenly recovered. So my cleansing was put off, on the grounds that if I lived I was bound to be defiled again, and the stains of sin after that washing would bring greater and more dangerous guilt. I already believed then — and so did my mother, and the whole household, except my father. But he did not win out over the strength of my mother's devotion in me, so as to make me an unbeliever as he still was. For it was her great care that you, my God, should be my father rather than he; and in this you helped her to prevail over her husband, whom she, the better of the two, obeyed — and in obeying him she was also obeying you, who had so commanded.

I beg you, my God, I long to know, if it is your will: why was my baptism put off just then? Was it for my good that the rein was, so to speak, loosened on me, to let me sin? Or was it not loosened? If not, then why does it still ring in our ears on every side — "Leave him alone, let him do as he likes, he isn't baptized yet"? And yet, where bodily health is concerned, no one says, "Let him be wounded worse, he isn't healed yet." How much better, then, had I been healed at once, and my soul's recovered health kept safe, with my friends' help and my own, in your keeping, who gave it. Far better, truly. But how many great waves of temptation seemed to hang over me after boyhood! My mother foresaw them, and chose to expose to them the clay from which I might later be shaped, rather than the finished cast.

In boyhood itself, though — so much less feared on my behalf than the youth to come — I did not love study, and hated being forced to it. Yet I was forced, and this was done well to me, though I did not do well; for unless forced, I would not have learned. But no one does well against his will, even if what he does is good. Nor did those who forced me do well — but the good that came to me came from you, my God. For they cared nothing for how I might use what they forced me to learn, except to feed the bottomless appetite of a rich beggary and a shameful glory. But you, by whom the very hairs of our head are numbered, used for my good the error of all who pressed me to learn, and my own error, in refusing to learn, you used to punish me — a fitting penalty for one so small a boy and so great a sinner. So through those who did not do well you did well for me, and through my own sin you justly punished me. For you have commanded, and so it is, that every disordered love is its own punishment.

But why did I so hate Greek, which I studied as a boy? I still do not fully know. For I loved Latin — not the lessons of my first teachers, but what the so-called grammarians taught me. Those first lessons — reading, writing, and arithmetic — I felt to be as heavy a burden and penalty as any Greek. And where did this come from, too, but from the sin and emptiness of this life, since I was flesh, and a breath that goes and does not come back? Those first lessons were certainly better, because surer: by them I gained, and still keep, the power to read what I find written and to write what I want. The others forced me to memorize the wanderings of a certain Aeneas, forgetting my own wanderings, and to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love — while I, with dry eyes, endured my own miserable self dying among these things, far from you, O God, my life.

For what is more miserable than a miserable man who has no pity on himself — who weeps for Dido's death, dying for love of Aeneas, but does not weep for his own death, dying for want of love for you, O God? You, light of my heart; you, bread of my inmost soul; you, the Power that gives vigor to my mind and quickens my thoughts — I did not love you. I committed adultery against you, and all around me, in the same adultery, voices cheered, "Well done! Well done!" For friendship with this world is adultery against you, and the "Well done! Well done!" goes on until a man is ashamed not to be one of the crowd. And for all this I did not weep — I who wept for slain Dido, who "sought by the sword her bitter, mortal wound" — while I myself sought the bitterest, lowest end among your creatures, having forsaken you, earth slipping back into earth. And if I had been forbidden to read all this, I would have grieved that I could not read what grieved me. Such madness is thought a higher and richer learning than the lessons by which I learned to read and write.

But now, my God, cry aloud in my soul, and let your truth tell me, "Not so, not so. That first study was far better." For look — I would more readily forget the wanderings of Aeneas and all the rest than how to read and write. True, there is a curtain hung over the door of the grammar school — yet this is not so much a sign of something hidden as a cloak for error. Let them not cry out against me, those I no longer fear, while I confess to you, my God, whatever my soul wills, and find peace in condemning my own bad ways, that I may love your good ways. Let neither the buyers nor the sellers of grammar-learning cry out against me. For if I ask them whether it is true that Aeneas once came to Carthage, as the poet says, the less learned will answer they do not know, and the more learned that he never did. But if I ask how the name "Aeneas" is spelled, everyone who has learned it will answer me rightly, according to the signs men have agreed on by convention. And if I ask which could be forgotten with less harm to one's life — reading and writing, or these poetic fictions — who does not see what everyone must answer, unless he has utterly forgotten himself? So I sinned, as a boy, when I preferred those empty studies to the more useful ones — or rather, loved the one and hated the other. "One and one is two"; "two and two is four" — this was to me a hateful singsong, while "the wooden horse packed with armed men," "the burning of Troy," and "Creusa's ghost, her sad and shadowy likeness" were the chosen spectacle of my vanity.

Why then did I hate the Greek classics, which tell the same kind of tales? For Homer too is skilled at weaving such fictions, and is most sweetly empty — and yet he was bitter to my boyish taste. And so, I suppose, Virgil would be to Greek children, forced to learn him as I was forced to learn Homer. The difficulty — yes, the difficulty of a foreign tongue — splashed bitterness, like gall, over all the sweetness of the Greek story. For I understood not one word of it, and to make me understand I was driven hard with cruel threats and punishments. There was a time, too, when as an infant I knew no Latin; yet I learned it without fear or pain, by mere observation, amid the caresses of my nursery and the laughter of friends, who smiled and played and urged me on. I learned it without the pressure of any punishment, for my heart pressed me to bring its own thoughts to birth, which I could only do by learning words — not from those who taught me, but from those who talked with me, in whose ears I was likewise giving birth to whatever I conceived. There is no doubt, then, that a free curiosity has more power to make us learn these things than a fearful compulsion. Yet this compulsion checks the wanderings of that freedom, by your laws, my God — your laws, from the schoolmaster's cane to the martyr's trials — being able to mix for us a wholesome bitterness that calls us back to you from the deadly pleasure that lures us away.

Hear my prayer, Lord; let not my soul faint under your discipline, nor let me faint in confessing to you all your mercies, by which you have drawn me out of all my worst ways — so that you may grow sweeter to me than all the allurements I once chased; that I may love you with all I am, and clasp your hand with my whole heart, and that you may yet rescue me from every temptation, all the way to the end. For look, Lord, my King and my God: let whatever useful thing I learned as a child be put to your service — that I speak, write, read, and reckon for your service. For you gave me discipline while I was learning empty things, and the sin of delighting in those empty things you have forgiven. In them, I admit, I learned many a useful word — but those can just as well be learned in things that are not empty, and that is the safe path for the steps of the young.

But woe to you, torrent of human custom! Who can stand against you? How long until you run dry? How long will you keep rolling the sons of Eve into that vast and dreadful ocean, which even those who climb the cross can barely cross over? Did I not read in you of Jove the thunderer — and the adulterer? Both he could not truly be; but the pretended thunder was invented to give cover and license to real adultery. And now, which of our gowned masters lends a sober ear to a man who cries out, from their own school, "These were Homer's fictions; he brought human things up to the gods — if only he had brought divine things down to us!" Truer still would he have said, "These are indeed his fictions, but he gave a divine nature to wicked men, so that their crimes might no longer count as crimes, and whoever committed them might seem to be imitating not abandoned men but the gods of heaven."

And yet, you torrent of hell, into you the sons of men are thrown, with rich rewards, for mastering such learning; and a great ceremony is made of it, conducted in the public square, in full view of laws that grant a salary on top of the students' own fees. And you lash your rocks and roar, "Here words are learned; here eloquence is learned, so necessary to get your way and to win your arguments." As if we would never have known such words as "golden shower," "lap," "beguile," "the temples of heaven," and the rest of that passage, unless Terence had brought a worthless youth onto the stage, setting up Jupiter as his model for seduction —
"Gazing at a painting where the tale was told / of Jove sending down a golden shower / into Danaë's lap, a woman to beguile" —
and then see how he stirs himself to lust as if by heavenly warrant:
"And what god? The great one / who shakes the highest temples of heaven with his thunder.
And I, a poor mortal man, should I not do the same? I did it, and gladly I did it."

The words are learned no more easily for all this filthiness; rather, by means of the words the filthiness is done with less shame. I do not blame the words — they are like choice and precious vessels — but the wine of error that drunken teachers pour out for us in them; and if we do not drink it too, we are beaten, with no sober judge to whom we may appeal. And yet, my God — in whose presence I can now remember this without harm — all of it, sadly, I learned willingly and with great delight, and for it I was called a promising boy.

Bear with me, my God, while I say something of my cleverness — your gift — and the follies I wasted it on. I was set a task troubling enough to my soul, with praise or shame and the fear of a beating riding on it: to speak the words of Juno as she raged and grieved that she could not
"turn this Trojan prince away from Italy" —

words I had heard that Juno never said; but we were made to wander in the footsteps of these poetic fictions and to say in prose roughly what the poet had said in verse. And the boy whose speech won most applause was the one in whom the passions of rage and grief stood out most strongly, dressed in the most fitting words, keeping up the dignity of the character. What is it to me, my true life, my God, that my speech was applauded above so many of my own age and class? Is not all of it smoke and wind? Was there nothing else for me to exercise my wit and tongue on? Your praises, Lord — your praises might have propped up the still tender shoot of my heart with the support of your Scriptures, so that it would not have trailed away among these empty trifles, a defiled prey for the birds of the air. For there is more than one way in which men sacrifice to the rebel angels.

But what wonder that I was carried away to empty things and went out from your presence, my God, when the men set before me as models were these: men who, if they made some slip of grammar in telling of an action of theirs that was not in itself bad, were ashamed when corrected — but who, when they told of their own disordered lives in rich, polished, well-ordered words, and were praised for it, gloried in it? You see all this, Lord, and keep silent — patient, and full of mercy and truth. Will you keep silent forever? Even now you are drawing out of this horrible pit the soul that seeks you, that thirsts for your delights, whose heart says to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, will I seek. For to be far from your face is to be in the dark of disordered loves. It is not on our feet, or by changing place, that men leave you or return to you. Did that younger son of yours look for horses or chariots or ships, fly off on visible wings, or travel by moving his limbs, in order to squander in a far country all you had given him at his departure — a loving Father when you gave it, and more loving still when he came back with empty hands? So it is in lustful, that is, in darkened loves that the true distance from your face is measured.

Look, Lord God — and look patiently, as you always do — at how carefully the sons of men keep the agreed rules of letters and syllables handed down from those who spoke before them, while they neglect the eternal covenant of everlasting salvation that they have from you. So much so that a man who knows or teaches the inherited rules of speech will offend people more by saying, against the laws of grammar, "a uman being" without the breath of the h, than if, against your laws, he, a human being, hates a human being. As if any enemy could do him more harm than the hatred with which he burns against him; as if he could wound the man he persecutes more deeply than he wounds his own soul by hating him. Surely no knowledge of letters is as deeply woven into us as the record written on the conscience: that he is doing to another what he would hate to suffer himself. How hidden are your ways, O God — you, the only great One, who sit silent on high and by a tireless law deal out a blinding punishment to lawless desires! A man chasing the fame of eloquence, standing before a human judge, ringed by a human crowd, raging at his enemy with the fiercest hatred, will watch most anxiously that no slip of the tongue lets him "murder" the word "human being" — and takes no care at all that, in the fury of his spirit, he does not murder a real human being.

This was the world at whose gate I lay, poor wretch, in my boyhood; this was the arena where I feared more to commit a grammatical blunder than, having committed one, to envy those who had not. I say and confess these things to you, my God — the things for which I was praised by those whom it then seemed the whole of virtue to please. For I did not see the pit of vileness into which I had been flung, away from your eyes. In their sight, what was fouler than I already was, displeasing even people like myself, deceiving my tutor, my masters, and my parents with countless lies, all from love of play, an itch to watch worthless shows, and a restlessness to act them out myself? I committed thefts, too, from my parents' cellar and table, driven by greed, or to have something to give the boys who sold me their play — which all the while they enjoyed no less than I did. And in this play I often sought to win by cheating, mastered all the while by an empty craving to come out on top. And what could I bear less, and rebuke more fiercely when I caught it, than the very thing I was doing to others? And if I was caught and rebuked for it myself, I would rather pick a fight than give in. Is this the innocence of boyhood? Not so, Lord, not so — I cry for your mercy, my God. For these very sins, as the riper years come on, pass over from tutors and masters, from nuts and balls and pet sparrows, to magistrates and kings, to gold and estates and slaves, just as harsher punishments take the place of the cane. It was the small stature of childhood, then, that you our King commended as an emblem of lowliness, when you said, Of such is the kingdom of heaven.

And yet, Lord — to you, the Creator and Governor of the universe, most excellent and most good — thanks were owed to you, our God, even if you had granted me boyhood only. For even then I existed, I was alive, and I had feeling; I had within me a care for my own well-being, a trace of that mysterious Oneness from which I came; I kept watch, by an inner sense, over the wholeness of my senses; and in these small pursuits, and in my thoughts about small things, I learned to take delight in truth, I hated to be deceived, I had a strong memory, I was furnished with speech, I was soothed by friendship, I shrank from pain, from baseness, from ignorance. In so small a creature, what was not full of wonder, full of praise? But all these are gifts of my God; I did not give them to myself. They are good, and all together they are myself. Good, then, is he who made me, and he is my good; and before him I will exult for every good I had as a boy. For this was my sin: that I sought my pleasures, my heights, my truths, not in him but in his creatures — in myself and others — and so fell headlong into sorrows, confusions, and errors. Thanks be to you, my joy and my glory and my confidence, my God — thanks be to you for your gifts; but keep them for me. For so you will keep me, and the things you have given me will be enlarged and made perfect, and I myself will be with you, since even my existence is your gift.

Now I want to call to mind the ugliness of my past, the corruptions my soul fed on the flesh — not because I love them, but so that I may love you, my God. I do this for love of your love, going back over my most wicked ways in the very bitterness of remembering, so that you may grow sweet to me: you, sweetness that never fails, blissful and sure sweetness, gathering me again out of the scattering in which I was torn to pieces, when, turned away from you, the one Good, I lost myself among many things. For in my youth I had burned to be filled with the things below, and I dared to run wild with these tangled, shadowy loves. My beauty wasted away, and I was rotten in your eyes, while I pleased myself and longed to please the eyes of men.

And what was it I took such delight in, except to love and be loved? But I did not keep love within its measure, mind to mind, the bright border where friendship ends. Out of the muddy craving of the flesh, out of the bubbling-up of youth, a fog rose and clouded my heart over, so that I could not tell the clear brightness of love from the haze of lust. Both boiled in me, confused together, and swept my unsteady youth over the cliff of unholy desire and sank me in a gulf of disgraces. Your anger had gathered over me, and I did not know it. I had been deafened by the rattling chain of my mortality — the punishment of my soul's pride — and I strayed further from you, and you let me go. I was tossed about, spilled out, scattered, boiling over in my fornications, and you held your peace, O you my joy so slow in coming. You held your peace, and I wandered further and further from you, into more and more barren fields where only sorrows grow, in a proud dejection and a restless exhaustion.

If only someone, back then, had eased my disorder and put the fleeting beauties of these things — the outermost edge of your creation — to good use, and set a limit to their pleasure, so that the tides of my youth might have cast themselves up on the shore of marriage, if they could not be calmed; that the restlessness might have been kept within the purpose of raising a family, as your law prescribes, O Lord — you who shape even the offspring of this our dying, and can with a gentle hand blunt the thorns shut out of your paradise. For your power is not far from us, even when we are far from you. Otherwise I should have listened more carefully to the voice from the clouds: "Such will have trouble in the flesh, but I would spare you," and "It is good for a man not to touch a woman," and "The unmarried man thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but the married man cares about the things of this world, how he may please his wife."

I should have listened to those words more closely, and made myself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and waited more happily for your embrace. But I, poor wretch, foamed like a storming sea, following the rush of my own tide, abandoning you, and broke past every one of your limits. Yet I did not escape your lashes — for what mortal can? You were always with me, mercifully severe, sprinkling the bitterest taste over all my forbidden pleasures, so that I might go looking for a pleasure with no bitterness in it. And where to find that, I could not discover, except in you, O Lord — you who teach by sorrow, and wound us in order to heal, and kill us so that we will not die away from you. Where was I, and how far an exile from the joys of your house, in that sixteenth year of my body's life, when the madness of lust — which human shamelessness is given free rein to, though your law gives it no license — took command of me, and I handed myself over to it completely? My family meanwhile took no trouble to save me from falling by marriage; their only concern was that I should learn to speak well and become a persuasive speaker.

That year my studies were on hold. After I came back from Madaura, a nearby town where I had gone to study grammar and rhetoric, the money was being gathered for a longer journey to Carthage — gathered more by my father's determination than his means, for he was only a poor freeman of Thagaste. Who am I telling this to? Not to you, my God, but in your presence to my own kind, to that small share of humankind who may come upon these writings of mine. And why? So that whoever reads this may consider out of what depths we have to cry to you. For what is nearer to your ears than a heart that confesses, and a life of faith? Everyone praised my father for furnishing his son with everything needed for a long journey for the sake of his studies, far beyond what his means allowed — for many far wealthier citizens did no such thing for their children. Yet this same father gave no thought to how I was growing toward you, or whether I was chaste, so long as I was rich in speech, however barren I might be of your cultivation, O God, the one true and good Lord of your field, which is my heart.

But while in that sixteenth year I lived at home with my parents, free of school for a while — an idle season forced on us by the narrowness of my parents' fortune — the briars of unclean desire grew rank over my head, and there was no hand to root them out. And when my father saw me at the baths, now growing into manhood and clothed in a restless youthfulness, he was delighted, as if already imagining grandchildren, and gladly told my mother — rejoicing in that surge of the senses by which the world forgets you, its Creator, and falls in love with your creature instead of with you, drunk on the invisible wine of its own self-will, turning aside and bowing down to the basest things. But in my mother's heart you had already begun your temple and laid the foundation of your holy dwelling, while my father was still only a catechumen, and that only recently. So she was shaken with a holy fear and trembling, and though I was not yet baptized, she was afraid for me of those crooked paths walked by people who turn their backs to you and not their faces.

O misery — and dare I say that you held your peace, my God, while I wandered further from you? Did you truly hold your peace toward me then? And whose were those words, if not yours, that you sang in my ears through my mother, your faithful one? Nothing of them sank into my heart so as to make me act. For she wished — and I remember her warning me privately, with great anxiety — that I should never commit fornication, and above all never defile another man's wife. These struck me as womanish bits of advice that I would have blushed to obey. But they were yours, and I did not know it. I thought you were silent and that it was only she who spoke — she through whom you were not silent to me, and in whom you were despised by me, her son, the son of your handmaid, your servant. But I did not know it, and ran headlong with such blindness that among the boys my age I was ashamed to be less shameless. I heard them boasting of their disgraces, and the more degraded the boast, the louder it was, and I took pleasure not only in the act but in the praise of it. What deserves blame, if not vice? Yet to escape blame I made myself out worse than I was, and where I had not sinned as the lost ones had, I would claim I had done what I had not done, so that I would not seem contemptible for being more innocent, or cheaper for being more chaste.

Look at the company I kept as I walked the streets of Babylon and wallowed in its mire as though in a bed of spices and costly perfumes. And to make me stick faster at its very center, the invisible enemy trod me down and seduced me, for I was easy to seduce. The mother of my flesh, who had by now fled the heart of Babylon but lingered in its outskirts — even she, though she urged chastity on me and had heard from her husband what I was becoming, did not think to rein it in within the bounds of married love, if it could not be cut away to the quick. She did not see how dangerous all this was, both now and for what was coming, because she was afraid that a wife might prove a weight and a hindrance to my prospects — not the hope of the world to come, which she rested in you, but the hope of learning, which both my parents were too eager for me to gain: my father because he had next to no thought of you, and only empty notions of me; my mother because she reckoned that the usual course of studies would be no obstacle, but even some help, toward reaching you. So I gather, recalling as best I can what my parents were like. Meanwhile the reins were slackened on me past all proper firmness, to spend my time in amusement, even in dissolution, in whatever I fancied. And over all of it lay a fog, cutting me off, O my God, from the brightness of your truth, and my wrongdoing burst out as if from sheer fatness.

Theft is punished by your law, O Lord, and by the law written in human hearts, which not even our wrongdoing can erase. For what thief will put up with another thief? Not even a rich thief will bear with one who steals out of need. Yet I wanted to steal, and did, driven by no hunger, no poverty, but by a glut of well-being and a bloated craving for sin. For I stole something I already had plenty of, and far better. I did not even want to enjoy what I stole — I enjoyed the theft and the sin themselves. There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit that was nothing special to look at or to taste. Late one night — having dragged out our games in the streets till then, as our rotten habit was — a gang of us reckless young fellows went to shake the tree and carry off the pears. We took huge loads, not to eat, but to fling to the pigs, after barely tasting a few. We did it purely to do what was forbidden, simply because it was forbidden. Look at my heart, O God, look at my heart, which you took pity on at the bottom of the bottomless pit. Now let my heart tell you what it was looking for there, that I should be evil for nothing, with no cause for my malice but malice itself. It was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own undoing; I loved my falling-away — not the thing I fell toward, but the fall itself; my disgraced soul falling away from your firmament into utter ruin, seeking nothing through the shameful act but the shame itself.

There is a certain beauty in lovely bodies, in gold and silver and all such things; in the touch of the body there is a powerful answering pleasure, and each of the other senses has its own object fitted to it. Worldly honor too has its appeal, and the power to win and to master, out of which springs also the thirst for revenge. Yet to get any of these we must not turn away from you, O Lord, or stray from your law. The life we live here has its own charm, by a certain proportion of its own and a fitness to all the beautiful things below. Human friendship, too, is sweet, bound by a dear tie, for the way it makes one out of many souls. It is over these things and the like that sin is committed, when through an unchecked leaning toward these lowest goods, the better and higher goods are abandoned — you, our Lord God, and your truth, and your law. For these lower things have their delights, but not like my God, who made them all; for in him the righteous one delights, and he is the joy of the upright in heart.

So when we ask why a crime was done, we do not believe the answer unless it appears there might have been some desire to gain one of those things we called lower goods, or some fear of losing them. For they are beautiful and pleasing, though set against the higher, blessed goods they are cheap and low. A man has murdered another — why? He loved his victim's wife, or his estate; or he wanted to rob him to live; or he was afraid of losing something to him; or, wronged, he was on fire for revenge. Would anyone commit murder for no cause at all, taking simple delight in the killing? Who would believe it? Even that wild and savage man who was said to be cruel and evil for nothing — even for him a cause is given: "so that hand and heart should not grow slack through idleness." And to what end? So that, by all that practice in crime, he might seize the city and gain office, power, and riches, and be free of the fear of the law and the strain of his debts at home and the knowledge of his own villainy. So not even Catiline loved his own crimes — he loved something else, and that was why he did them.

What, then, did wretched I love in you, my theft, my deed of darkness, in that sixteenth year of my life? You were not beautiful, since you were theft. But are you anything at all, that I should speak to you like this? The pears we stole were beautiful, because they were your creation, you the most beautiful of all, Maker of all, good God, God the highest good and my true good. The pears were beautiful, but it was not them my miserable soul wanted — I had a store of better, and I picked these only in order to steal. Once I had picked them, I threw them away; my whole feast was my own sin, and that was what I took pleasure in. If any bit of those pears did pass my lips, what sweetened it was the sin. And now, O Lord my God, I ask what it was in that theft that delighted me. Look — it has no loveliness. I do not mean such loveliness as there is in justice and wisdom; nor as in the mind and memory and senses and animal life of a person; nor the glory of the stars, beautiful in their courses; nor the earth and sea, teeming with new life that replaces by birth what dies away. It has not even that false and shadowy beauty that belongs to the deceiving vices.

For pride too plays at being lofty, while you alone are God lifted high over all. Ambition — what does it seek but honor and glory, while you alone are to be honored above all, and glorious forever? The cruelty of the powerful wants to be feared, but who is to be feared except God alone, from whose power what can be torn or kept back, and when, or where, or to where, or by whom? The caresses of the lustful want to pass for love, while nothing is more tender than your love, and nothing is loved more wholesomely than your truth, bright and beautiful above everything. Curiosity puts on the look of a thirst for knowledge, while you supremely know all things. Even ignorance and stupidity hide under the name of innocence and harmlessness — because nothing is found more single than you, and what could do less harm, since it is the sinner's own deeds that harm him? Sloth wants to look like rest, but what steady rest is there except in the Lord? Self-indulgence longs to be called plenty and abundance, but you are the fullness and the never-failing abundance of pleasures that do not rot. Extravagance throws up a shadow of generosity, but you are the most overflowing Giver of every good. Greed wants to own many things, and you own all things. Envy fights for first place — but what is higher than you? Anger goes after revenge — but who takes revenge more justly than you? Fear shrinks from things strange and sudden, threats to what it loves, and takes thought for their safety; but to you what is strange or sudden, and who can separate from you what you love, and where, except with you, is safety unshakable? Grief wastes away over things lost, the delights it craved, because it would have nothing taken from it — as nothing can be taken from you.

So the soul commits fornication when it turns away from you and seeks outside you what it cannot find pure and clean until it comes back to you. All who go far from you and rise up against you are imitating you in a twisted way. But even by imitating you like this, they show that you are the Maker of all that is, and that there is nowhere they can go to get away from you entirely. So what did I love in that theft, and how was I, even corruptly and perversely, imitating my Lord? Did I want, by stealth, to do something against your law — because I could not do it by power — so that, a prisoner, I might act out a crippled freedom, doing what was not allowed me with no consequence, a darkened likeness of your all-powerfulness? Look at the servant running from his Lord and catching nothing but a shadow. O rottenness, O monstrous life and depth of death — could I love what was not allowed, for no reason except that it was not allowed?

What shall I give back to the Lord, that my memory can call these things up and my soul is not terrified by them? I will love you, O Lord, and thank you, and confess to your name, because you have forgiven me these great and wicked deeds. To your grace I credit it, and to your mercy, that you melted my sins away like ice. To your grace I credit, too, whatever evil I did not do — for what might I not have done, I who loved a sin for its own sake?
